opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think "world models" is one of those terms that means very different things depending on who you ask, so it helps to be a bit precise.

There's the narrow, classical definition from RL and robotics: a model that predicts how an environment evolves given some action, so you can plan or imagine rollouts instead of interacting with the real world all the time. That's a well-defined thing, and it's useful.

Then there's the much broader, almost philosophical use of the term: does the model have an internal representation of how the world works? Physics, causality, other agents, common sense. People argue about whether language models "have" a world model or are "just" predicting the next token. Honestly, I find that framing a bit of a false dichotomy. If you're really good at predicting the next token across the whole internet, you're forced to compress a lot of structure about the world. Whether you call that a world model is partly semantics.

More recently, people mostly mean video and interactive generation: models that produce a consistent, controllable environment you can walk around in. That's exciting, and the visual results are impressive. But my personal take is that pixel fidelity isn't the interesting bar. What matters is whether the model captures the right abstractions, things like object permanence, consistency over long horizons, and the ability to respond to interventions in ways that make sense. You can have something that looks beautiful and still doesn't really understand what's going on.

So I think of world models less as a separate category of model and more as a capability axis. Every good foundation model is some kind of world model. The real questions are: in what modality, at what level of abstraction, and is it useful for downstream reasoning and action? I'm somewhat skeptical of the idea that you need a fundamentally different paradigm to get there. A lot of it might just fall out of scaling the right data, the right objectives, and especially more interaction and feedback rather than passive observation.

r001.rationale: The response says “world models” means very different things depending on whom you ask, signaling that the overall concept lacks a single well-defined meaning, while noting that one narrow definition is well-defined.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "world model" has become one of those terms that means very different things depending on who's saying it. For some people it's the Ha and Schmidhuber sense, a learned simulator you do planning inside of. For other people it's basically a vibe, like "the model understands physics." And then there's the camp that says language models can't have a world model because they only see text.

My take is kind of boring, which is that I don't think the distinction is as clean as people want it to be. If you train a large enough model on enough data with the right objective, it has to build some internal representation of the generative process behind that data, because that's the cheapest way to predict well. Whether you want to call that a world model is more a naming debate than a technical one. Next token prediction over text is already modeling a world, it's just the world as mediated by humans writing things down. The text isn't the world, sure, but it's a very dense compression of it.

Where I think the term actually earns its keep is when you're talking about something explicit and actionable. Can the model roll forward state? Can you take actions in it and get consistent consequences back? Does it stay coherent over long horizons instead of drifting? That's a real capability gap, especially for anything embodied or for agents operating in environments where you can't just retrieve the answer. Video and interactive generation work is interesting to me for that reason, not because it's a different kind of intelligence, but because the consistency requirement is so much stricter than text. You can hand-wave in prose. You can't hand-wave when the cup has to still be on the table two seconds later.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that you need a separate module labeled "world model" bolted onto the architecture. My bias from the scaling side is that a lot of this falls out of the right data mix and the right objectives at scale, and the modularity people draw on whiteboards tends to blur in practice. But I'll admit I hold that loosely. The honest answer is we don't have great ways to measure how good a model's internal world model actually is, so a lot of the debate is people arguing about something nobody can see directly.

r001.rationale: The response says “world model” means different things to different people and that the distinction is not clean, clearly conveying that the concept is not well-defined.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by a world model. If you mean a model that learns how the world works and can predict what happens next, then language models already do some of that. To predict text well, you need to learn something about the processes that produce that text—people, objects, cause and effect.

But there’s a stronger definition where the model can predict how an environment changes when you take an action. That’s a more specific capability, and being good at predicting text doesn’t automatically establish that you have it.

So I would think about it in terms of capabilities rather than labels. Can the model predict consequences? Can it handle a situation it hasn’t seen before? Can it use those predictions to make better decisions? Those are the things that would make a world model useful.

r001.rationale: The response says the answer depends on what is meant by “world model” and distinguishes a broad definition from a stronger one, communicating that the concept lacks a single well-defined meaning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by a world model. In a broad sense, a language model already has to learn something about how the world works to predict text well. It needs some representation of people, objects, cause and effect. But that’s different from saying it has a faithful simulator of the world inside it.

The more useful question for me is: what can you do with that representation? Can you predict what happens after an action? Can you reason about a situation you haven’t seen before? Can you use it to plan, and then update your understanding when reality disagrees?

So I tend to think of world models as a spectrum rather than a separate category of model. Predicting language gives you some aspects of the world; learning from actions and observations might give you others. What matters is whether those representations support reliable predictions and decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says the answer depends on what one means by “world model” and describes it as a spectrum rather than a separate category, communicating that the concept lacks a single clear definition.
